(Text) :
The victory of our principles in the present situation when the world is divided into two camps depends in a large measure upon the dynamism of our democracy. The essential truth of democracy must capture the hearts of men all over the world if human civilization is not to be destroyed in wars and revolutions far more terrible than anything that has yet been endured. Canada, as a first contribution to the crusade for democracy, could offer our democratic principles for the drafting of an international declaration of human rights and fundamental freedoms which could be accepted by the nations of the world as a guidance in their domestic legislation and international relations.
Recently, in April of this year, a group of individuals representing liberal thought in nineteen nations, alarmed by the danger of communist oppression, have decided to come together for the purpose of "winning general acceptance of democratic principles and to foster a free society based on freedom and personal responsibility, and to provide means of collaboration between men and women of all countries who agree with these principles."
At a meeting held at Oxford of what was called the Liberal world union or the Liberal international as opposed to the red international, these opponents of socialist fascist and communist parties, desiring to express in
Human Rights

words democratic and liberal ideals, adopted a manifesto containing the following principles:
(I)
1.	Man is first and foremost a being endowed with the power of independent thought and action, and with the ability to distinguish right from wrong.
2.	Respect for the human person and for the family is the true basis of society.
3.	The state is only the instrument of the community: it should assume no power which conflicts with the fundamental rights of the citizens and with the conditions essential for a responsible and creative life, namely:
Personal freedom, guaranteed by the independence of the administration of law and justice.
Freedom of worship and liberty of conscience.
Freedom of speech and of the press.
Freedom to associate or not to associate.
Free choice of occupation.
The opportunity of a full and varied education, according to ability and irrespective of birth or means.
The right to private ownership of property and the right to embark on individual enterprise.
Consumer's free choice and the opportunity to reap the full of the productivity of the soil and the industry of man.
Security from the hazards of sickness, unemployment, disability and old age.
Equality of rights between men and women.
4.	These rights and conditions can be secured only by true democracy. True democracy is inseparable from political liberty and is based on the conscious, free and enlightened consent of the majority, expressed through free and secret ballot, with due respect so the liberties and opinions of minorities.
(II)
1.	The suppression of economic freedom must lead to disappearance of political freedom. We oppose such suppression, whether brought about by state ownership or control or by private monopolies, cartels and trusts.
We admit state ownership only for those undertakings which are beyond the scope of private enterprise < ( in which competition no longer plays its part.
2.	The welfare of the community must prevail and must be safeguarded from the abuse of power by sectional interests.
3.	A continuous betterment of the conditions of employment, and of the housing and environment of the workers is essential. The rights, duties and interests of labour and capital are complementary; organized consultation and collaboration between employers and employed is vital to the well-being of industry.
(HI)
Service is the necessary complement of freedom and every right involves a corresponding duty. If free institutions are to work effectively, every citizen must have a sense of moral responsibility towards his fellow men and take an active part in the affairs of the community.
(IV)
War can be abolished and world peace and economic prosperity restored only if all nations fulfil the following conditions:
(a)	Loyal adherence to a world organization of all nations, great and small, under the same law and equity, and with power to enforce the strict observance of all international obligations freely entered into.

(b)	Respect for the right of every nation to enjoy the essential human liberties.
(c)	Respect for the language, faith, laws and customs of national minorities.
(d)	The free exchange of ideas, news, goods and services between nations, as well as freedom of travel within and between all countries, unhampered by censorship, protective trade barriers and exchange regulations.
(e)	The development of backward areas of the world with the collaboration of their inhabitants in their true interests and in the interests of the world at large.
Mr. Speaker, there is very little in the declaration I just read with which the true democrats of the Canadian parliament would not agree, except for the fact that it does not mention God as the source of all rights and freedoms. I suggest, however, that the declaration be studied by the committee and I submit respectfully that it would at least form a sound basis for discussion in the committee.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was dealing with the terms of reference applicable to the proposed committee. Certain of the speakers in the debate this afternoon made some interesting points. The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) in particular pointed out a fact that we should not lose sight of, that under the British constitution the principle of the supremacy of parliament is the important principle, that parliament may make any laws it wishes, may confer rights, may alter rights or may even deprive individuals of rights by its act. He pointed out also that that principle has been extended to the British dominions and that in the Dominion of Canada this parliament is supreme within the sphere of its jurisdiction and the provinces are supreme within the spheres of their jurisdictions.
That being true, the adoption of the other system, the system of constitutional limitations upon the powers of parliament, would be a radical departure from the principles which have heretofore applied. It would be an introduction into our system of a feature of the American institution; it might possibly be called an Americanization of our constitution. When I say that I am not prejudging the case or the issue as to whether it would be desirable, because that is a matter within the sphere of the terms of the reference which the committee, if it thinks fit to take up this question of a bill of rights, will be free to decide.
I was approaching the point in my remarks where I felt it would be necessary to consider carefully just what is meant by the adoption of a bill of rights for the Dominion of Canada. I am not sure whether the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) favours the adoption of a constitutional amendment or merely the enactment of a dominion statute. On page 3152 of Hansard, of May 16, I find this passage from his speech:
It was for that reason that I suggested, and now suggest, that, when this committee is set
up, representatives from the various provinces be convened here, so that by joint action a comprehensive bill of rights may be evolved either by way of constitutional amendment or by statute.
I should like to consider for a few moments just what the case would be as respects the dominion and the provinces and the relations between the dominion and the provinces if the first alternative were adopted, that is, the enactment of a constitutional amendment. The only way in which our constitution may be amended is by an amendment to the British North America Act. As all members of this house know, under the British North America Act property and civil rights are within the jurisdiction of the provinces. The first observation I should like to make is that if our constitution is amended by the enactment of sections comparable with those in the American constitution severe limits would be placed upon the field of jurisdiction now delegated to the provinces. I think it is well that the house should realize that and should understand it thoroughly.
The theme has been laboured, particularly within the last few months in this house, that the dominion should not invade the jurisdiction of the provinces. If the constitution is amended in this way it would mean that the right of the provinces to legislate as they think fit in the field of civil rights would be limited and curtailed. The principle of provincial legislature supremacy in the field of civil rights would no longer exist. It may be that my hon. friend favours the other alternative, that of a dominion statute. When I turn to page 3158 of Hansard I find this passage from his speech:
Individual civil liberties, those that we have inherited today, guard the weak against the strong. What is needed are civil liberties by declaration of parliament which will guard the individual against the state. It might be argued that another government, another parliament, can revoke a bill of rights passed by parliament. True; but has not history shown that when laws are put upon the statute books, having the support of a vast majority of the people, they stay there?
A declaration of a bill of rights in the country would be a positive declaration on the part of men and women of all political faiths in their belief in civil liberties. Whether the federal authority has the power or not to pass legislation respecting civil liberties, its passage would strengthen the hand of the Minister of Justice in the matter of the disallowance of any statute which would deny freedom anywhere in our country.
In other words, it is suggested that it might be desirable to pass a dominion statute, whether or not we have jurisdiction to pass that statute, affecting as it would civil rights, and then use the statute as a basis for the disallowance of provincial statutes which
Human Rights

might be passed from time to time in conflict with the dominion statute. There, again, I think the house should understand the implications of that proposal. The practice of the disallowance of provincial statutes, while r.ot wholly uniform and perhaps not entire!}' settled, is more or less so and, generally speaking, the dominion authorities respect the rights of the provinces to legislate within their constitutional field.
It is a somewhat serious proposal that the dominion government should pass an act somewhat regardless of whether it has the power to pass it, affecting as it would civil rights, and then use that act, whether constitutional or unconstitutional, as the basis for the disallowance of acts passed by the legislatures of the respective provinces. I want to say again that I am not prejudging the case; I am a member of the committee, and I do not intend to take a position in this matter in this house in advance of the discussion in the committee. But I do want to point out to this House of Commons the seriousness of these proposals and their radical nature.
The hon. member for Lake Centre then dealt with a miscellaneous assortment of proposals with respect to specific statutes. These proposals were not necessarily tied up to his bill of rights proposals, but I should like to say a few words with regard to those and the amendment or repeal of individual statutes. The hon. member for Rosthern mentioned two of those proposals this afternoon. One was that fiats be abolished, that so far as the dominion government is concerned, and that is as far as we can go, we should do away with the necessity of obtaining a fiat.
This matter arose in this house a few weeks ago and I stated that, so far as I was concerned, I had an open, mind on that proposal. I will go farther and say, not only on my own, behalf but on behalf of the government, that we have no objection to that proposal. When I say that I want to say that, so far as we are concerned,, the proposal has little or no practical importance, because I have made inquiries and find that during the last twenty years never has a fiat been denied except in an admittedly frivolous case, and I do not know whether there have been many or even any of those. Persons who desire to bring actions against His Majesty the King in the right of Canada are granted fiats automatically unless, as I say, the action is of a patently frivolous nature. So from a practical point of view it does not matter whether we abolish or continue fiats in the. dominion field. I see no objection, whatever to abolishing fiats and, if the committee and the house wish to do it-I
would not want to get the matter into controversy because the issue is not one of practical importance-the government would have no objection to introducing the necessary legislation, but I would hope that we would not be asked to do it until next year because of the lack of practical importance of the issue involved.
The other matter mentioned by the hon. member for Rosthern this afternoon and also by the hon. member for Lake Centre was an extension of the appellate powers of the Supreme Court of Canada. That is a question which requires study. If and when appeals to ^he judicial committee of the privy council from the Dominion of Canada are abolished the whole question of the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of Canada will have to be carefully reviewed. At the present time except in criminal cases Canadians have the right to apply to the judicial committee of the privy council for leave to appeal in all cases. They do not have the same rights in the Supreme Court of Canada, and it may be necessary, it may be desirable, to extend the appellate jurisdiction of the supreme court and to make the necessary amendments to the Supreme Court Act. That is a matter which could properly be studied by the committee if the committee considers that it is of importance commensurate with that of the other subjects of great importance which it will have to consider.
Another act which the hon. member for Lake Centre mentioned as being one which perhaps ought to be amended or revamped, I think was the word he used, is the Public Inquiries Act. The point about the Public Inquiries Act is just this, that witnesses are not as such entitled to counsel in proceedings before a royal commission. The relevant sections of the Public Inquiries Act are these:
12.	The commissioners may allow any person whose conduct is being investigated under this act, and shall allow any person against whom any charge is made in the course of such investigation, to be represented by counsel.
13.	No report shall be made against any person until reasonable notice shall have been given to him of the charge of misconduct alleged against him and he shall have been allowed full opportunity to be heard in person or by counsel.
Under these sections a witness before a royal commission is entitled to counsel if a charge is made against him in the course of the investigation, and he is entitled to counsel and to reasonable notice before any report is made against him so that he may attend with counsel. These provisions were at the time the act was passed, I think in 1912, regarded as adequate. The point which has been raised recently, as a result probably of the espionage

Fluman Rights
inquiry, is not a new one. The point was fully discussed in the debates of the day in 1912 or 1913, and it will be found that Sir Robert Borden, after an open-minded discussion of the issues involved, advised the house that, in his opinion, these safeguards were adequate. It may be argued that they should be extended; it may be argued that they are sufficient. If the matter comes before the committee that is set up, the debates of that day and much other material available on the subject will be of great value to the committee. But that again is a matter pertaining to the amendment of a specific act of parliament rather than a part of a bill of rights.
Another act that was mentioned was the Official Secrets Act. It is suggested that the Official Secrets Act is too hard on the accused, that certain presumptions of guilt should be removed from the Official Secrets Act. If that position is put forward in the committee I think anyone who puts it forward will find some pretty strong reasons for the present provisions of the Official Secrets Act. The presumption of innocence is, it is true, an old and highly prized right. It has been found necessary, however, in much provincial legislation and in some of our dominion legislation to reverse or remove this presumption in particular circumstances. Nearly every session there comes before the house legislation which precipitates a debate as to where the onus should lie. The only point I am making is that no general or universal rule can be laid down. I do not know that anybody would advocate that all the presumptions of guilt in the Official Secrets Act be reversed. The presumption was reversed in the Official Secrets Act of Great Britain, and it has been in our own. It would be prejudging the case to say that our present act is perfect, but it is also prejudging the case to say that it should be changed because the presumptions are reversed in certain circumstances.
There are in this world a great many highly ntelligent persons who have made a careful study of our British system of law and procedure with certain objects in mind. Those objects are to take full advantage of the rules, so that they can carry on espionage within Canada with impunity. Persons who are real offenders against the Official Secrets Act are persons who are selling out and betraying their country. Spies are not likely to leave much evidence behind them, either direct evidence or circumstantial evidence. Their methods are developed so as to capitalize, to the full, presumptions of innocence, necessity of proof beyond reasonable doubt, necessity of corroboration and all the other rules which
have been worked out through the centuries as safeguards of liberties by courts and legislators who had in mind crimes very different from the kind of crimes that spies commit. Consequently the provisions to which my hon. friend objects were enacted for the protection of the state and of the liberties which the existence of a democratic state provides. It may be that some changes in this legislation are desirable; but if the question is raised in the committee the committee will have to decide how far we dare tamper with legislation which has been forced upon us by pressure of modern espionage methods.
Then, I come to the War Measures Act. While I have stated carefully that I do not wish to prejudge any of the proposals which have been put forward, it is almost impossible for me not to prejudge that one. The proposal is that the War Measures Act be repealed. The wording used by my hon. friend is this:
I have a few suggestions to make. The first one is that this committee should consider the advisability of the repeal of the War Measures Act, which has been on the statute books since 1914. In between the first and the second wars, on several occasions in the House of Commons a declaration was made that it was no longer in effect. That act, standing as it does, constitutes an invitation to any government in the future under the emergency theory to declare an emergency to the detriment of the rights of our people.
Then there followed some questions and interjections, following which the hon. member for Lake Centre said:
My right hon. friend says it was a very necessary act. It was necessary in the period of the war; but in the days of peace, with the challenge that the state is making to the rights of the individual, Professor Lower supports the stand that I take, namely, that the act should be repealed.
I should like the house to understand the seriousness of that suggestion, namely, that the War Measures Act be repealed. The War Measures Act was passed in 1914, and has remained on the statute books ever since. It remains dormant unless there is a war, insurrection or apprehended war. It is admitted by the hon. member-and, I think, by everybody else in Canada without exception-that the War Measures Act is necessary in time of war.
The proposal seems to be that we wait until there is a war before we pass it, that we repeal it now and then wait until there is a war before we put it on the statute books again. I do not know how that proposal appeared to hon. members, but in a country the size of Canada and with the possibility that if we got into a war again that war
Human Rights

would burst upon us with great suddenness, would we not be taking an entirely unwarranted gamble in the time factor if we were to take the War Measures Act off the statute books of this country?
An American general, I believe it was Major-General Russell P. Groves, said not so long ago that the first few hours of surprise assault in another war might cost the lives of forty million Americans. I do not know whether that is so or not. But it is because I do not know, and because none of us knows, it would be extremely serious to make it necessary for parliament to be called together before the necessary legislation could be enacted for the carrying on of a war.
And then, think of all the things which have to be done when the war clouds are gathering. Before the last war, the defence of Canada regulations were in course of preparation for at least six months before the war came, because during the summer of 1939 it looked as if war were coming. Those regulations could not have been prepared, except under an act, and that act was on the statute books of Canada.
The same is true of regulations respecting foreign exchange control, respecting trading with the enemy, respecting dependents' allowances and various other regulations which were prepared in advance, so that, if war did come, we would not be caught napping. And they all had to be prepared under the War Measures Act. If those persons who were working on those regulations did not know what kind of act they would have, or whether they would have any act at all, or what the provisions of the act would be, how could they possibly place themselves in a state of readiness for any conflict which might possibly come?
It might be said that if it looked as if war were looming up we could put the act on the statute books. But I think if hon. members will consider the proposal they will see some pretty serious objections to it. If Canada were to enact a War Measures Act in anticipation of a war, it might be extremely prejudicial to our international relations. In effect, it would be a declaration that we were expecting a war. It would be interpreted, probably, as a declaration that we wanted a war. The economic effects; the effects on markets and on the prices of commodities and on government financing would have to be taken into consideration, if an act were passed such as the War Measures Act in anticipation of a war, when there was still a hope that such a war might be avoided.
[Mr. Ilsley.l
That act was passed in 1914, and it was left on the statute books of this country between the wars. Now some well-meaning professors come along and write treatises say^ ing that we should repeal it. And the hon. member for Lake Centre identifies himself with that proposal. As I said before, I do not want to prejudge anything which may take place in committee; but it is pretty hard not to prejudge such a proposal as that.
I now come to another matter which has been discussed at length in the press, and which my hon. friend discussed at some length in his speech. I refer to the espionage inquiry. My hon. friend says in that connection:
I come down to a more recent example, and that is in connection with the espionage commission set up under order in council passed on October 6, 1945.
May I interject at this point that the commission was not set up under the order in council of October 6, 1945. It was set up in February, 1946, but the order authorizing the detention and interrogation of those who were believed to have the information about espionage was passed on October 6, 1945. Then the hon. member continues:
No one today would say that there was not in that order in council a cavalier disregard of great and basic constitutional liberties, of those liberties which my right hon. friend says are guaranteed to all our people under the charter of British peoples.
Much has been said in criticism of the action the government took with reference to the espionage inquiry. And little, I must say, has been said on the other side. I have received some letters from persons who were concerned about the methods which were adopted, and who have protested about them. I have tried to point out to my correspondents, as I should like to point out to the house, certain vital facts which I think it is high time were pointed out.
It should be pointed out that, while measures of an exceptional nature were taken in the investigation of the Gouzenko charges, the situation was one of grave and acute emergency. The government had reason to believe that information of a most important kind, including information relating to the atomic bomb, was disclosed to a foreign power by persons connected with Canadian governmental activities. Apart altogether from the other kinds of information that were being communicated, the communication of information about the atomic bomb might have had the most far-reaching and devastating consequences. Anyone who has read much about the effects of the atomic bomb-a book, which, I believe, is called "Hiroshima" is a

Human Rights
good example-which include the agonizing suffering and mass destruction of men, women and children, must realize the appalling consequences which might have flowed from the flouting by government servants of governmental policies in relation to secrecy in this field; and from violation of oaths of secrecy, and from violation of the Official Secrets Act. Let us not forget that we were not confronted with any ordinary situation at all. We were confronted with an extraordinary one.
While exceptional steps were taken to bring into the open conspiracies which we had reason to believe existed, and which have since been proved to have existed, there are certain facts which should be borne in mind. One is that every step taken by or on behalf of the government was legal. The report of the royal commission clearly establishes this fact. To hear a great deal of the criticism made, one would have thought we in some way violated the Habeas Corpus Act or we had broken certain laws. As the hon. member for Rosthern pointed out this afternoon, however, no order in council was passed that was not authorized by legislation of this parliament. We operated under the authority of this parliament, and the royal commission operated under the authority of this parliament in every step it took.
The second fact is that no one denies the capacity or sense of responsibility of the royal commission itself.
There has been some criticism of the government for selecting two judges of the Supreme Court of Canada as royal commissioners, but I would like to point out to the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), who is very strong on this point, that there are certain great and grave situations wherein it is not inconsistent with the dignity of a judge, nor is it inconsistent with the duties of the judiciary for them to act as royal commissioners, and that fact has been recognized in the old country as well as in this country for a great many years. Here, if ever, there was a case where the public must be satisfied of the impartiality of the commissioners and of the reliability of their findings, and therefore we felt we were completely justified in going to the highest tribunal in the land and taking two judges from that court and setting them up as a royal commission.
No one denies the capacity or sense of responsibility of the eminent counsel who conducted the investigation before the commission. One of them was president of the Canadian Bar Association at the time, and the others were men of character and capacity, and a deep sense of responsibility.
No one denies the gravity or emergent character of the situation to be dealt with. No one denies the desirability of dealing with the situation effectively. No one denies that the investigation might very well have been a fiasco had not such steps been taken.
In this event, if it had been a fiasco, we would today have been assured by those who are attacking us that the investigation was a mere witch hunt, that the bogey of communism had once more been falsely raised, and that Gouzenko's stories were merely figments of the imagination. That is what we would have been told today, and this is borne out by the avidity with which critics of the government seize upon every acquittal to prove that the prosecution of the person acquitted was unjustifiable, a conclusion which is invalid, as I shall try to show in a few minutes.
So much by the way of background of the position we took. I am not going into all the charges, accusations and grounds of criticism of the government and of the royal commission; they are pretty well answered in the report of the royal commission itself. But it is said that we should not be circulating that report, and it is said in particular that a certain note which the government authorized to be placed in a statement appended to the report should not be circulated.
Let me read what my hon. friend says on that latter point, and this is something which I feel like almost indignantly repudiating. On page 3156 of Hansard, he says:
I abhor communism and all its works, but the added words signify an attitude that no government should display. They indicate a spirit of resentment because the courts of the country saw fit not to allow the declaration of a royal commission.
Canadians have the right not to be deprived of life, liberty or property without process of law. Should they not also have the right not to be deprived of reputations by an executive that is exasperated by the results in the courts? That addendum by the government condones the lawless enforcement of the law.
Let me tell the house, in case they have not been following this matter, what the addendum was. A report was published and, as I shall argue in a few moments, it was not only our right but our duty to circulate that report. Certain of the persons reported against were tried in the criminal courts and were acquitted. We felt that, in fairness to
Human Riahts

them, the fact of their acquittals should be communicated to those who received the report, and so we put in the front of the report a statement that certain persons had been acquitted. But we made this addendum:
It must not be assumed that in any case the evidence before the commission and that adduced at the criminal proceedings were the same.
It is that addendum which makes some critics see red-I am not trying to make a pun on the word "red." It makes them very angry because they say it is unfair to the accused. If we had not added it, the fact that we were publicizing the acquittals would be taken as a criticism or perhaps a repudiation of the work of the commission, and it was certainly far from our wish to express any criticism of that kind, for reasons which I shall state.
I think the answer to what my hon. friend says there, and to similar forms of criticism, can be given to the house most concisely by my reading a letter which I wrote to one of the civil liberties associations with whom I have an enjoyable correspondence, the civil liberties association of Manitoba. That asso-cation, on the 28th day of April, sent me a resolution which was in the following terms:
1.	That the Canadian government be requested to repudiate the note added to the report of the royal commission on espionage and dated January 30, 1947, reading:
"It should not be assumed that in any ease the evidence before the royal commission and that adduced in the criminal proceedings were the same."
This statement is not only unfair to persons acquitted in the recent trials but also implies contempt for the law of Canada as administered in the courts.
2.	That the Canadian government be requested to withdraw from circulation the report of the Kelloek-Taschereau royal commission.
Upon receiving that letter, I replied-

It is signed by David Owens, secretary, civil liberties association; and my
reply is addressed to David Owens, secretary, Civil Liberties Association of Manitoba. It reads as follows:
Ottawa, 10th May, 1947.
Dear sir,-
I have your letter of April 28, 1947, advising me of the contents of a resolution recently adopted at a general meeting of the Civil Liberties Association of Manitoba. This resolution requests that the Canadian government withdraw from circulation the report of the Kelloek-Taschereau royal commission. I am of opinion that I would not be justified in recommending that this be done.
_ This commission, as you know, consisted of two judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, the highest court in the land. They were assisted bycounsel of equally high standing in their profession, one of whom was the president of the Canadian Bar Association. The proceedings were conducted with care and fairness and every witness was given the fullest opportunity to tell his story and explain all circumstances which appeared in any way to reflect upon him. The result of this investigation is a report of immense value to the nation. To deny such a report to the public because some of the witnesses were later acquitted after prosecution would be in my opinion unwarranted.
Is it not possible that the difference between the purpose and nature of the proceedings before the royal commission and the purpose and nature of the proceedings before the criminal courts has been overlooked? The royal commission was not a court having criminal jurisdiction. Its findings were based upon preponderance of evidence, while those of the criminal courts were based upon proof or lack of proof beyond reasonable doubt. The commission in the report, after setting out the evidence adduced before them, stated its opinion as to what certain witnesses and others did. There is no reason why this opinion should not be presented to the public together with a statement of the grounds upon which the opinion was based. It is open to the public to decide whether or not the opinion arrived at was a correct one.
It must be kept constantly in view that the report disclosed a most serious conspiracy to furnish secret information to a foreign power and that subversive elements had infiltrated into the public service on a considerable scale. In a matter of such vital importance to the whole Canadian public, it would be, in my judgment, indefensible to withhold from publication the commission's report of the steps it took and of the conclusions it arrived at. The withdrawal of the report from circulation would, I believe, be an undemocratic suppression of information to which the public is entitled.
The resolution passed by your association also requests that the Canadian government repudiate the note added to the report reading: "It should not be assumed that in any case the evidence before the royal commission and that adduced in the criminal proceedings were the same." The allegations advanced for this request are two in number: First, that the statement is unfair to persons acquitted in the recent trials, and secondly, that the statement implies contempt for the law of Canada as administered in the courts.
I regret to say that I am unable to agree that either of these allegations is correct. There are, in my opinion, good reasons for the addi-

Human Rights
tion of the note in question. It -was recognized that upon acquittals taking place, it would be only fair to those who were acquitted to state that fact to those receiving the report. The statement setting out the acquittals was therefore added and circulated with the report. This statement, however, would _ have been incomplete and misleading had it not contained a note to the effect that the acquittals were not necessarily based on the same evidence which was adduced before the commission. The note might even have gone further and pointed out that the rules of procedure and the evidentiary principles upon which findings were based were necessarily different. In any event, had the note not been added, those receiving the report might very well have come to the conclusion that the government was, by pointing out the fact of the acquittals, criticizing or repudiating the work of the commission, which the government was and is far from wishing to do.
The government regards the work of the commission as having been immeasurably beneficial to the interests of Canada. The commission did its duty and did it well, just as the courts did their duty and did it well. The commission was set up for one purpose, the courts functioned for another. The rules of evidence and procedure were not the same, the evidence itself was not necessarily the same, and a belief in the propriety of the steps and action taken by the commission is in no way inconsistent with a belief in the propriety of the steps and action taken by the courts.
I am unable to understand the following sentence in the resolution referred to in your letter: "This statement is not only unfair to persons acquitted in the recent trials, but also implies contempt for the law of Canada as administered in the courts." For the reasons which I have stated, I do not regard the statement as unfair to the persons acquitted in the recent trials, nor can I agree that it implies any contempt for the law of Canada as administered in the courts.
I accept your statement that your association in no way condones subversive activity, but I must observe that the withdrawal from circulation of the report of the commission as requested by your association, while not condoning subversive activity, would make the climate more favourable to the growth of subversive activity and remove a formidable barrier to its spread.
Yours very truly,

I come now to a part of the speech made by the hon. member for Lake Centre, in which he quotes with approval certain statements of Professor Lower, as reported at page 3156 of Hansard, one of which is as follows:
The conduct of government, from Prime Minister to royal commission, over the espionage case, bore every appearance of hysteria, when it did not bear the appearance, as unfortunately in certain quarters it did, of sheer persecution.
This raises the important question: Should the concern which the government felt over the disclosures of Gouzenko be characterized as hysteria, or was it the type of grave concern which the people of Canada expect from a government having a deep sense of responsibility for the welfare of its citizens, the preservation of its institutions and the future of the state? If hon. members think that the proper word to describe the state of mind of the government was "hysteria" rather than "responsible concern", then the hon. member for Lake Centre has made out a strong case against the government. But if they feel that the concern we displayed was justified, then there is no case against the government, but on the contrary there is the strongest of all possible cases for the government. As for myself, I believe that our concern was justified to the hilt. I believe that if we had not taken prompt, vigorous and effective measures, we should have been recreant to our trust. The government of Canada, by resolutely investigating and bringing to light the shocking facts revealed in the espionage inquiry, rendered an immense service, not only to the people of this country, but to those of other democratic countries. The view now put forward-and apparently with approval-by the hon. member for Lake Centre is that we became too excited. One would almost think, to hear this view, that, after all, this was not an important affair. But I am satisfied' that is not the view taken either by the rank and file of the Canadian people or by responsible observers abroad. We have been attacked for the manner in which the investigation was conducted, but some of this attack has been a manifestation of party politics. I confidently assert to this house, from conversations I have had with many Canadians in all walks of life, that far from the public resenting the steps taken by the government, they endorse those steps. It is all very well for opposition critics and arm-chair critics, now that the offenders are brought to justice, the plots exposed and the public of democratic countries put on the alert, to indulge in criticism of this, that or the other step which was taken; but these opposition critics would have sung a very different song if, as a result of our public service not having been cleansed of subversive elements, the drive against our institutions and our liberties had gone unchecked. We had a grave responsibility to shoulder. We assumed that responsibility and are prepared to defend the course we took, both here and elsewhere.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution before us calls for the nomination of a com-
Human Rights

mittee on human rights and fundamental freedoms, which would also seek the best way to fulfil certain obligations entered into by all members of the united nations organization.
In this materialistic age of ours, the terms right, justice and freedom are in some quarters strangely misused. Some so-called master minds construe them so as to cover all sorts of errors and abuses. They claim the freedom to do everything they please as if such a right were admitted, in a well-organized Christian society. For them, a right is a means to any end. They would establish the principles of a new justice, or rather injustice, to do away with social order, to deny God, divine and natural laws, to substitute a pagan state to the Almighty Himself, who is the source of all good and therefore of all rights and freedoms.
I wish to protest against this materialistic and pagan trend. Allow me to say briefly what are, to my mind, freedom, and right and justice.
To be free does not mean to have one's own way with everything, to such a pass as to exalt evil to a system and to legalize injustice. To be free does not mean to organize opposition to God and persecution against His ministers, to deprive man of his faith in God. To be free does not mean to tolerate open warfare against God and the state which is the dispenser of justice from above. Freedom is the right man has to act for the good and not for evil. Liberty is the right to act, for temporal motives, according to human dignity and to the dictates of one's reason, which implies the respect of the rights and property of others, and for spiritual motives, which represent the ultimate end of man.
Indeed, if liberty means the right to do anything why then adopt a bill of rights? If such a bill is not based upon the recognition of God, how can we adopt principles consistent with His justice? If we are not agreed upon the, basic principle of the authority of the state, which consists in enforcing respect for God, private property and social order, what would be the value of declarations which will substitute licence and revolution to true freedom?
Therefore, it is necessary to distinguish as between freedom of worship and the antisocial and anti-religious propaganda of certain sects whose tracts are filled with libels and blasphemies. Those anarchists demand freedom of religion but at the same time they defy the divine and human laws and spread hatred against the Catholic, Protestant and Jewish religions. Far from being advocates of true liberty, they are the fanatical partisans of licence and anarchy. I do not agree 
with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Hiefenbaker) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-what a strange combination-in regard to the meaning of freedom of worship.
Jehovah's Witnesses and similar sects are entitled to their beliefs, but let them not deny other citizens the same privilege Let them show regard for the law and the religious convictions of the majority and all will be well. As crown prosecutor for the province of Quebec, I have had to read some of their pamphlets that were a tissue of abuse and blasphemy, repeatedly condemned by our criminal courts. Whenever such people transgress the laws of the land, provincial governments can only summon them before the courts as in the case of any other lawbreakers, and no one should seek to derive some political advantage out of a situation such as that. I don't see why an exception should be made, in the name of freedom, in favour of the very ones who disregard it and attempt, by libel and falsehood, to spread discord and hatred in a country like ours where peace, order and charity should be the rule. Man is not free to sow hatred; for he then abuses liberty which entitles him to act for the good and not for the destruction of society.
Who will claim that a member of society has a right to destroy the other component parts of that body? Right is everyone's due. Justice is that virtue which inclines the will to a recognition of the rights of others.
It is surely neither right nor justice to trample upon one's oath of allegiance or to betray one's country. A Canadian's first duty is to seek his country's welfare. Any deviation from this sacred duty must not only be punished but prevented by all means at the government's disposal.
I, therefore, congratulate the Government for having taken energetic measures to fight communism. A spy ring had been organized and constituted a menace to our country's security. A number of subversive acts were denounced and names were brought to the executive's attention. What was the duty of our government? According to the hon. member for Lake Centre, we should have refrained, for the sake of freedom, from interning those who were suspected of designing against the very existence of the Canadian nation. For the sake of this so-called freedom, were we to permit a group of enemies in our midst to maintain communications with certain foreign powers, to the prejudice of Canada?

Human Rights
Mr. Speaker, not only was the government entitled to do so, but they were in duty bound to stop, by all available means, the activities of a group suspected of jeopardizing our constitutional and social freedoms. It was a duty on a plane far superior to the temporary physical freedom of an individual against whom suspicions have not led to a conclusive proof.
I hope our bill of rights will never allow a traitor to enjoy his freedom while he is a menace to the majority of our citizens.
It is therefore imperative that in the Canadian bill of rights the divine as well as the temporal rights be safeguarded against any encroachment by enemies of Christian faith and social order.
Would it not be necessary, on that occasion, to ensure more protection for the rights of certain citizens and of the racial groups which are the very foundation of this country? As a matter of fact, the structure of our nation has been built up by French- and Englishspeaking Canadians; they have the same rights and it behooves them mutually to respect them, especially as regards language, education and religion. Therefore, I feel that complete recognition of those rights would go a long way toward the achievement of perfect unity in this country.
In the province of Quebec, the Englishspeaking minority enjoys, from the standpoint of education, the same rights and privileges as the French-speaking majority. Mr. Speaker, there is no reason why this principle should not be observed in all provinces toward the French-speaking minority. Let this principle be written into the charter of our rights and let the provinces accept all its implications by ratifying it. That is a ground of dominion-provincial understanding which no province would have the right to ignore. In so saying, I am neither raising prejudice nor rousing passions.
On the contrary, I claim, in the name of true liberty and plain justice, a right which is no doubt recognized by an overwhelming majority of this country's citizens. It is through mutual recognition of those fundamental rights that we shall make Canada a Christian democracy whose influence will extend throughout the world.
Mr. Speaker, let us be realistic and sincere. Our liberties rest upon the ten commandments which constitute a charter for free men in a Christian society. We must draw from true principles of charity the boundaries of freedom, that is the right to act legitimately for our own good and that of our fellow-citizens. Let us do justice unto others as we would wish upon ourselves and there will be room in this
Canada of ours for all men respectful of divine, natural and civil laws. I hope that our country will never give shelter to the traitors, the anarchists and the ungodly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house has listened with interest and profit to the sober statement of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley). I have never criticized, either openly or otherwise, the action of the government in the espionage trials. I had my doubts, my fears and my reservations in regard to the procedure, but I did not know how much the government knew and consequently I felt that I was not in position to judge as to what they had done. On the other hand, I did not criticize those who were criticizing the government, because I felt that 'that was their right. But I did feel that there was a little too much criticism in the espionage cases when one took into consideration the lack of criticism in a case which I felt was much more important, where not just a mere handful of people were concerned but where several thousands were concerned. Several thousand Canadians had their freedom interfered with, their property rights taken away, and there was very little heard about the matter.
The persons concerned in the espionage cases were brought to trial and some were found guilty, which was justification to some extent for 'the action the government had taken. Others were found not guilty. But they had their day in court, while these other people to whom I refer, Canadians of Japanese origin, have not had their day in court up to this day. So I felt all along that too much attention was given to the one ease and not sufficient to the other. In reality, the circumstances, that is the interference with freedom, was 'the same in both cases. If it was wrong to take away the freedom, at least for a short time until they were convicted or released, of the few concerned in the espionage cases, surely it was wrong in the case of the people of Japanese origin.
What I wanted to speak about tonight and my reason for taking part in the debate is to say that during the course of the debate I felt that the fundamental principles underlying human rights and human freedoms were not very much discussed. In my opinion, the basis of freedom is equality; where there is no equality freedom is limited. My reading of history leads me to believe that history down through the ages is largely a struggle of the working class to throw off the yoke of its exploiters and masters. The growth and extension of democracy have been brought about by
Human Rights

new classes coming up and taking part in the government. By such process has democracy been extended.
Much has been said about Magna Carta. Magna Carta in reality conferred freedom on but a small segment of the population of England of that time. The great mass of the English people were yet beyond its benefits, and indeed not for centuries down through the industrial revolution and even until 1874 when universal suffrage for the male population was adopted in Britain did the mass partake of the benefits of democracy.
I have here "British History in the Nineteenth Century", by George Macaulay Trevelyan, a noted historian, from which I quote a paragraph or two to indicate the position of the working class in Britain around 1795. At page 158 of this book, the author says:
The Tory panacea for unrest had been proclaimed in 1795 by Bishop Horsley when he said that "the mass of the people had nothing to do with the laws but to obey them."

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Why not?

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Because they had nothing to do with the laws. They did not have the franchise. They had no part in the administration of their country's affairs. As the reverend bishop said-, all they had- to do with the law was to obey it, and that remained the situation for a considerable time after that. So those who think that liberties and freedom are being curtailed are in my opinion, away off the mark. I do not believe that liberties and freedom are being curtailed, I believe that liberties and freedom are being extended every day. That is not to say that we should not be careful of those liberties and concerned to preserve them. To continue the quotation from Mr. Trevelyan, he says at page 159: Citizens, indeed, the workmen were not. They had no word in the government of England, and no civic position in the local area which they had come to inhabit. If they happened to be lodged within a chartered town, they lived under a close corporation and its municipal magistrates. If they were outside such precincts, they were under the rural justices of the peace and the antiquarian relics of the court leet. Neither urban nor rural authorities were called upon to provide for health, lighting, decency or education in a new factory quarter. They were content to quell riots and to arrest trade unionists, sedition-ists, deists, frame-breakers and other criminals.
For a long, long time after, that was the position of the working class in England, but that is not their position today, and they are not treating their so-called superiors in the way their own class had been treated for so many centuries.

Along the same lines I have another quotation from "The British People, 1746-1946," by G. D. H. Cole and Raymond Postgate. It covers the period from 1746 to 1946, and referring to the position of the industrial workers in Britain and more particularly to children of a tender age, the- authors say:
To this early period of labour shortage belongs the "parish apprenticeship" system, under which many thousands of children from London and other large towns, having become inmates of pauper institutions, were shipped in droves to the new factory areas, there to be bound apprentices to some cotton lord who undertook to feed and clothe them in a barrack built specially for their occupation, and even to give them a minimum of schooling in his factory school. This system, which, as we have seen, Peel's "first Factory Act" of 1802 was designed to bring under some sort of regulation, died out rapidly as soon as local supplies of child labour became available; for the factory owners soon found that "free" labour, which they could engage and discharge at will, came cheaper than pauper labour which they were bound to maintain throughout the period of apprenticeship, whether trade was good or bad. In bad times, the "free" factory children had to be kept by their parents, or out of the local poor rates, of which the factory owners paid only a relatively small part.
Those were the conditions in Britain for many, many years. How different in Great Britain today, under that "terrible" socialist government, where the welfare of the children is the first concern of the state.

I did not have the good fortune to go to a university, but I will back my philosophy and my ability to state it against the hon. member's any day, also its correctness in relation to present economic and social conditions. As I said before, as regards those who talk of losing our freedom if we are to have security, that is the philosophy of the well-to-do. We cannot have freedom unless we have security. We cannot have freedom in its fullness unless we have security.
A moment ago I said that equality was the basis, and the only basis, that freedom can have. In this country, in so far as there is division among us, that division arises because of certain people wanting a greater share of the goods they produce. Others fear that if those people do get a greater share of the wealth their labour produces they themselves will have to do with a smaller share.
That, after all, is the difference between us, largely, in the many industrial and the other disputes which arise between the various classes in the community. There is good ground for such disputes. The man who lives on an income of $5,000 or $10,000 has a great many things that the man who lives on an income of $1,000 or $1,200 or less does not have. Not only can the man with the income of $5,000 or $10,000 have certain things for himself, but he can do certain things for his children that the other man cannot do. And does anyone really think any man with spirit will see other children having things his children cannot have, without making a protest about it?
I have here a news item from the Ottawa Journal of May 6, 1947. It is a report of a speech made by Doctor G. E. I am not ,and I think no one else is in a position to say if a bill of rights should be passed

I spent some few years m that country and through that fact together with my reading, I am fairly conversant with what takes place over there. I do not think they have any more freedom or assurance ol freedom than we have in this country.
They passed numerous laws, besides the bill of rights itself, to protect the freedom of the individual. But instead of protecting the freedom of the individual, some of them have been used to protect the freedom of big business.
I hold in my hand a book entitled "The Folklore of Capitalism", by T. W. Arnold, who, I believe, was at one time either the attorney general or the assistant attorney general of the United States.

Mr. Arnold was referring to the due process of law in the United States constitution, the fifth amendment. The due process of law provides that no person shall be held to answer for a capital, or otherwise infamous crime, unless on a presentment or indictment of a grand jury, except in cases arising in the land or naval or other forces. And he pointed out that, instead of that amendment's now being used to protect the ordinary citizen, the ordinary trade unionist or other person who comes within the grip of the law, today-and this is what he says at page 34:
Today this amendment is one of the reasons why railroads are protected from a federal pension system. Public control of business becomes the same as taking away property. Great national organizations become individuals.
We cannot in my opinion, base our assurance of enjoying freedom on a statute or as part of the constitution.
I think the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) would argue that there are sufficient safeguards in our laws to protect the people who were mixed up in the espionage cases. But it is clear that those statutes did

not save them. I am certainly convinced that there were laws to protect the persons of Japanese origin who were removed so ruthlessly from their homes on the Pacific coast. And yet it was not done.
Our liberties, regardless of what is in the law, can never be safe unless we are ever watchful that nothing shall interfere with them.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is to be commended for proposing the nomination of a committee on human rights and fundamental freedoms. I hope this motion will meet with great success.
But let us not delude ourselves. The standard definitions of freedom and human rights were coined centuries ago and have long since been embodied in the statute books of so-called civilized nations, where they lie dormant, save when the crash of guns breaks in upon their slumber.
Every time men are bent on devouring one another, those rights and freedoms provide material for tirades and slogans intended to whet the soldiers' mettle. But when the struggle is over, they don the shrouds which they had shed for a time, and men soon forget the destruction wrought in their name.
"All good maxims are in the world, but we fail only to apply them." Thus spoke Pascal, three hundred years ago.
The important thing, to my mind, is not therefore to seek new definitions, nor to enlarge the scope of our governing principles, nor yet to place a new legislation on our statute books, but to show Americans, Europeans and Asiatics how we Canadians make use of the freedoms secured through the valour of our pioneers, the heroism of our discoverers, the martyrdom of our missionaries and the blood of our soldiers. It is to act in such a way that our country set an example to the rest of the world, so that all may know that in North America, in this beloved Canada of ours liberty is respected by all, and that it is alive not only in our minds and in our hearts but also in the acts of our parliaments.
"Theories are not conducive to progress; they only lead to upheaval." We must not imitate Plutarch who beat his slave while writing fine speeches on morals, or Cicero who reproached himself with feeling too deep a sorrow upon the death of a beloved servant.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE

"Christianity with its dou trine of equality before God and human brotherhood caused the greatest moral upheaval among ancient communities" and set

Human Rights
free millions of slaves and Christianity will bring perfect happiness to modern society. If mankind is to survive it must heed the precepts set forth in the gospel by the Saviour and put into practice the divine commandment: "Love thy neighbour."
Liberty, Mr. Speaker, does not thrive upon empty talk and legal documents. It requires concrete facts, tangible acts, a sincere attachment and courageous men ready to carry its torch into all the homes of the world, from the richest to the poorest.
Liberty is dying today from the ridiculous misuse of its name; it is withering away from abuse in the hands of leaders of nations. In order to give it a radiant and' beaming life, it is necessary to apply strictly the sacred principles which make it so fine and so essential. It must be jealously guarded against abuse by those who, mistaking it for licence, turn it into anarchy. In heaven's name I hope that the new charter will not have the same lamentable fate as its famous predecessor, the Atlantic charter of April 14, 1941. Canada, with other allied countries, had also signed, on January 1, 1942, the famous declaration of the allied nations, which came out of the Churchill-Roosevelt agreement. What happened later on, to quote only one of the articles of the charter, clause 3, which provided that:
Their governments respect the right of all nations to choose the political system under which the latter shall live and desire restoration of the sovereignty and autonomy of those deprived of them by violence?
Who thinks today of that declaration, Poland enslaved by Russia, Czechoslovakia, Russia's satellite, Archbishop Stepinac's Yugoslavia, who all signed this solemn pact and are now prone under the muscovite yoke?
The Right Hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), referred last Friday to the many violations of the Magna Carta in Scotland, his native land. It would be interesting to recall here the many violations of our constitution of 1867 and the provincial liberties transgressed and tampered with in the last 80 years by the central power.
The government, which must set the example should respect and recognize provincial rights just as hon. members of this house should be consistent in granting others the same freedom they claim for themselves and in not denying their political opponents, outside this house, the right to disagree on certain matters and to fight for the triumph of their cause.
It is so easy and it takes so little courage to insult those who are absent and are immensely superior to their slanderers, that I am not surprised to see some hon. members take the opportunity of their contributing to
the debate or use the services of that hotbed of Liberal propaganda, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to attack those who, in spite of blackmail by the federal authorities, in spite of all sorts of threats and pressure by centralizers, stubbornly insist on defending the rights and freedom of the citizens they are committed to help and protect.

speechtext:
Before concluding, I wish to quote a few words from a highly respected patriot of our province, Canon Lionel Groulx. They show much better than I could do it myself the contribution made by the French Canadians in the preparation of an unwritten bill of rights in this country:	.
Never before in the civilized world have freedom, the rights of the human person and western humanism been discussed as much as they are at present. We French Canadians have not contributed quite as much as others to the greatness of our country in certain spheres, the commercial, financial and industrial, for instance, but no one has surpassed our common contribution to Canada's political or constitutional progress, to its climb towards freedom. One hundred years ago, our people were the first to disseminate the initial formulae of political liberty. Nowadays, we again remain in the van of the country's national aspiration towards a less theoretical independence and in its resistance to oppressive centralization. The achievement of Acadian and French-Canadian minorities in Canada has run a parallel course. The people of our race have fought and still suffer today; Why? Because they have refused to submit 'to the rule of might; because, true sons of freedom-loving ancestors, they have not stood for any encroachment upon their rights as fathers, men and citizens; because they believed in Christian equality of rights and refused to consider constitutions mere scraps of paper. I claim that such examples of courage and human dignity, though set by humble folk, none the less carry the stamp of grandeur and fruitfulness. These little people have done good service to the whole country. The fact must be proclaimed and will remain our exclusive glory as long as it is useful and fitting to resist oppressive state control as well as blind levelling powers that aim at standardizing the species; as long as clinging to the stars remains a lofty privilege, as long as we hold necessary to the life and greatness of the country reverence for those ancient ideals called spiritual values, that is to say, loyalty to one's cultural heritage, human freedom, justice and right.

Mr. NORMAN JAQUES (Wetaskiwin); I have listened to this debate with much interest, Mr. Speaker, but I cannot say that I feel very happy as a result of it. I have listened to the criticism from this side of the house. Unfortunately I do not understand the French language, so that I do not know what the French-speaking members have said. But I cannot agree with the criticism made of the Department of Justice and the royal commission for their part in bringing the spies to trial. I must say I do not quite see the purpose of this bill of rights. I do not quite see what is behind it. I do not know why Canadians should need to pass laws in this day and age for the purpose of securing the freedoms and human liberties. Who and what threaten our liberties today? The Canadian people have arrived at a state of freedom which, if it does not surpass, certainly equals the liberty of any people who have ever lived on this earth. It seems to me that what threatens the freedom of the Canadian people -and that of all other people for that matter- is nothing more or less than the threat of surrender of the sovereignty of this country. To those people who are so anxious to protect the liberties of the Canadian people, I put it to them to tell this house and the people outside this house how they intend to guarantee the freedom of the Canadian people when they propose to surrender that freedom to international control. That is What I should like to be told. Many hard things have been said of the procedure taken against the spies. I am not a lawyer, so that I am ignorant of legal terms and language; but many harsh things have been said about the actions of the commission and even of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Spies are not ordinary criminals. The ordinary criminal attacks individuals and he can be treated as such, because his threat is no more than a threat against an individual. But a spy is at war against the state; that is, he is at war against everybody in the state. It is true that some of the accused were afterwards found not guilty. I must say that I think it is curious that the longer the trials were continued, the bigger was the percentage of the accused who were released. I know there was an immense amount of pressure brought to bear. One hon. member-I think it was the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot)-obtained the information that outside pressure was being brought to bear in the interests of the accused; pressure from the United States, for instance. But even if some of the accused were found not guilty, is anyone

Human Rights
so naive as to think that people who chose as their intimate friends and companions above all others-as the accused did for years- persons who were afterwards convicted of spying, did not know what was going on? I cannot bring myself to believe such a story. Legal proof may have been wanting, but I have no doubt in my mind of their moral guilt.
I think that the people of this country owe an immense debt. Perhaps the greatest service that has ever been rendered to them, in peace time at least, was the service which was rendered by the Department of Justice, the royal commission and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police by exposing the spy ring. I should like to record my appreciation of the fact that at least some of these spies were brought to justice. If there was a mistake I think it was that the inquiry stopped short. There are plenty more, Mr. Speaker, who while they may not be committing legal offences, beyond question are working to undermine the faith and loyalty of the people of Canada, and such people have no right to be in the employ of this or any other government. I was glad when Mr. Ahearn, who, I believe, is not a politician, was moved to provide for Mr. Gouzenko's future. I think that was a fine gesture, and I should like to congratulate Mr. Ahearn on what he did. For let us consider that in spite of our Department of Justice and even despite our most excellent mounted police-and there is no finer police force in the world than the Royal Canadian Mounted Police-had it not been for Mr. Gouzenko, who was able to produce the legal evidence, these spies still would be at work selling out this country and the Canadian people. Therefore I say the Canadian people owe an immense debt to Mr. Gouzenko for what he has done.
With regard to the civil liberties organizations, there is no doubt that most of them are part of the communist front. I am not going into that aspect of the matter tonight; I make the statement, and I shall stay with it.

With regard to the civil liberties people, who are so anxious to assert and to parade their belief in liberty, let me quote from the report of the royal commission, at the bottom of page 223. I have quoted this before in the house, but I make no apology for quoting it again:
A statesman with every means of observation wrote in 1937:

That is a quotation from the book "Great Contemporaries," by the Right Hon. Winston Churchill.
I now come to what I think is the main point of this whole question. How were decent, honourable, loyal citizens converted into spies, so that they were not only willing but anxious to work against their own country? We have the answer in the report of the royal commission, and I am going to quote it at length, for I know that very few people outside this house have read this report. Here the commissioners are describing how these young Canadians were persuaded and twisted and turned from their loyalty to this country to become spies, and at the bottom of page 72 they say:
As the courses of study in the "cells" undermine gradually the loyalty of the young man or woman who joins .them, it is necessary to say something as to the content of the courses pursued in them, as that is reflected by the evidence.
The curriculum includes the study of political and philosophic works, some of them far from superficial, selected to develop in the students an essentially critical attitude towards western democratic society. This phase of the preparation also includes a series of discussions on current affairs, designed to further a critical attitude toward the ideals of democratic society.
But this curriculum would appear in reality to be designed not to promote social reform where it might be required, but to weaken the loyalty of the group member towards his or her own society as such.
Linked with these studies at all stages, moreover, goes an organized indoctrination calculated to create in the mind of the study-group member an essentially uncritical acceptance at its face value of the propaganda of a foreign state.
Accordingly the study groups are encouraged to subscribe to communist books and periodicals. The Canadian Tribune and Clarion of Toronto, Hew Masses (a periodical published in the United States). National Affairs of Toronto, and Club Life have been among those mentioned as regular objects of study and discussion in these groups, as well as selected books on Russia.

In some cases the effect of these study courses seems to be a gradual development of a sense of divided. loyalties, or in extreme cases of a transferred loyalty.
Thus it seems to happen that through these study groups some adherents, who begin by feeling that Canadian society is not democratic or not equalitarian enough for their taste, are gradually led to transfer a part or most of their loyalties to another country, apparently without reference to whether that other country is in actual fact more or less democratic or equalitarian than Canada.
Here is a paragraph which to me appears to be important:
Indeed, a sense of internationalism seems in many cases to play a definite role in one stage of the courses. In these cases the Canadian sympathizer is first encouraged to develop a sense of loyalty, not directly to a foreign state, but to what he conceives to be an international ideal. This subjective internationalism is then usually linked almost inextricably through the indoctrination courses and the intensive exposure to the propaganda of a particular foreign state, with the current conception of the national interests of that foreign state and with the current doctrines and policies of communist parties throughout the world.
Let me repeat one sentence:
In these cases the Canadian sympathizer is encouraged to develop a sense of loyalty, not directly to a foreign state, but to what he conceives to be an international ideal.
There is the whole reason for the intense opposition to what is now called nationalism. Nationalism is opposed to internationalism and, as long as a man believes in and stands for nationalism, his loyalty to his country cannot be undermined. That is the reason for the attacks on nationalists, not only in this country but in the United States. Those attacks always come from the communist front. That is why I am a nationalist and why I intend to stay a nationalist. It is the only protection against the modern form of disloyalty. It is the only protection that we have against a foreign state or a foreign ideology which has one purpose only, the enslavement of the world.
That puts a label upon all those people who have attacked nationalists as such, including myself as a so-called leader of nationalists in this country. I am a social crediter, and I am proud of it. That is my answer to those people who attack me, because I stand for Canadian nationalism which means loyalty to Canada and to the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy listening to a debate like this, which probably is a late result of the reconsecration week of six years ago. I do not know to what extent it will be profitable, but we hear fine expressions of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) calls good will. It is good will for all the nations of the world, and it is a good sign.
But if we are going back to the past, and if we think of what has happened even in this house, we might recall that seldom charity begins at home, and that some members of parliament are more inclined to say to others: "Do as I say, not as I do."
That is something which happens naturally during a war. It is a case of intermittent folly, and the intervals of lucidity are signalized by amnesia. It is a diagnosis I have often made; and I noticed that during the war there was only one way to think, a way contrary to that which has been expressed by the hon. member who has just spoken. During the war one was not permitted to say that he was a red-blooded Canadian. No; one had to be an imperialist; one had to be a colonial; one had to think only in terms of the British empire and the British commonwealth. That was the mental state, not only of one but of all during the war.
I do not know who has hypnotized my colleagues whom I like very much, but it was not only on this side of the house that that feeling existed. It was the feeling among all 
groups and parties, with few exceptions. And all seemed to be proud of that inferiority complex toward the empire and the commonwealth. Everybody was proud to be an empire serf or a colonial or commonwealth serf. They were glad of that; and in different language they were repeating what Lord Bennett said at the time he sailed for England, "I am going home"-when everybody was sending him elsewhere.
But that is what happened. During the war I was called a supporter of Hitler by those who were strong for the bill of rights, because I was defending the rights of the farmers, the railway men and those who were helping the war effort while working in overalls. During the war I was told by a cabinet minister that the only duty of a Canadian who was in good health was to enlist, thereby leaving aside all labouring men. And there was no protest in the house.

It reminds me of a story of the late Mr. Lapointe, at one time minister of justice. He was brought up in the country; he knew the [DOT]ways of living of the people, and he used to tell with great humour very fine stories that had a touch of philosophy. He had two friends in the county of Kamouraska. One of them was a client of mine. He was a notary public and his initials were T.M.T.-not T.N.T. He had a cousin there.
