Now we are going to reform them. It is purely academic. I find this debate frivolous 
and I find it futile. I said that once before on another occasion. I find that nothing will come out of it except expressions of good will which lead nowhere. This house must reform itself. We must not simply speak phrases. We must first set an example of good will, understanding, and tolerance to others. When a member of parliament is speaking here, some hon. members say, "Time, time," or "Quack, quack."

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: "Quack" yourself.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Well, I will tell my hon. friend that I will say that to him the next time he speaks and I shall be doing only as he has done. I have been most tolerant. I have not interrupted the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross). I have compassion for him. He shows the extent of his sincerity in supporting a bill of rights. There is no more intolerant man in this house than the hon. member for St. Paul's. He will support the bill of rights, and he will go to Toronto (St. Paul's) and say, "I am for the bill of rights." What rights? He will be unable to say, but he will be for that bill of rights.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Let the hon. member speak for himself, not for me.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE

If the hon. member gets angry it will be a good thing, because he is never so eloquent as when he loses control of himself.
One matter to which we should all give thought is that of discontinuing making speeches which amount to nothing.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: What were you saying about the debate in this house?

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is perfectly right when he speaks about platitudes, expressions of good will, being printed in the reports of these two sittings. We suffered a good deal. I remember one day when there was another chairman of the committee of the whole and when there was the assistant in Doctor Beauchesne's chair. My

Human Rights
case was clear. The chairman ruled in my favour, but a member of the cabinet winked and then he changed his ruling.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: He started a romance.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: He wanted me to apologize for saying that Ralston had put into my mouth words that I had never used. That was pretty tough, you know. And when I had to withdraw the expression "pompous" as applied to brass hats, it was also pretty tough.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: You bet.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
And it was the tougher because the request came from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). It is hard to realize how difficult it is for a private member to stand by his guns and be true to his convictions. even if he is wrong, provided that he is sincere.
As you know, sir, during the war exemptions were allowed for conscientious objectors, Mennonites, Hutterites, and Doukhobors; but after the farmers had been promised exemption from military service, they had1 to join the colours. A'ou remember the difficulty we had in trying to defend them just because there were some men in the army and in the department who thought that the duty of every Canadian was, as was stated in the house by the government, to join the colours. I am not anti-militarist any more than I am anti-British. But I find that it is a provocation of Russia to continue to consider her as a country which desires to wage war on Canada. I am not pro-Russian either. I am pro-Canadian. I am not any more pro-Russian than I am proBritish; and I am not anti-British either. But I consider Canada before England, Russia, France, China or any other country in the world. There was an investigation directed against the Russians, at the instigation of Igor Gouzenko. The evidence was obtained; the trials were very well prepared, and some of the accused people were found guilty. There were other arrests during the war. There was the arrest of Mr. Ohaloult, as well as of Mr. Drew. But proceedings against Mr. Drew were stopped. He did not undergo any trial, but Mr. Chaloult did. But the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), who came to the defence of Mr. Drew-and quite rightly -did not say a word in defence of Mr. Chaloult who had won his trial in Montreal. I will tell my hon. friend that I do not believe in the civil liberties league. I think those who are in all those leagues are just imposters who exploit human credulity and who are ready to defend scoundrels at the expense of honeist men. Moreover I will tell my hon. friend1 and you, Mr. Speaker, that during the 83166-207
war very discreetly I looked after a bitter Tory journalist from Toronto, as well as a French journalist from Montreal. I telephoned the offices of the Prime Minister and several other ministers so that no charge was laid against them. The memoranda against those two journalists were drafted by one who is a former member of the press gallery and one who is actually in the press gallery, but when I asked for that memoranda at the beginning of the session I could not get it; it was secret. I should like to have shown the insincerity of a man who is enthusiastic about the civil liberties league, who does not understand the problems of French-Canadians, and who betrayed the press gallery during the war, when I successfully defended it.
That is something. I never would have spoken of it if this debate had not taken place; but we have that intelligentsia which is a curse to the country. I am going to speak at home on Sunday about the future of youth, and I will tell youth that universities are to a large extent the cause of the unrest that exists in the country today. Young men are no longer taught to work from the bottom of the ladder and to climb gradually to the top, as former generations did. Young men are taught in social science courses and economics courses that they know all, that they are supreme, that they have nothing to learn, that they are ready to teach the world; and afterwards they try to organize for themselves, their families and their friends some fine nests where they will be comfortable while doing nothing and getting large amounts of money at the expense of the taxpayers of this country.
We have a lot to learn, but we have to come back to fundamentals. We cannot live on friends; we cannot live on declarations of rights such as those we have heard from all parts of the house. What does it amount to? My hon. friend said it-"Platitudes." And we listen to that. Today hon. members were anxious to come to this important debate about the bill of rights. In the first place, the discussion in this committee will be the cause of a great loss of time for the members, and the report will amount to nothing.
Before I conclude, I want to come back to what I was about to say. What I said had to be said by me, but I have more to say. Why take Russia, and say it is an enemy country, that those at the Russian embassy are spies? It may be true; I do not deny it, but why say that only about Russia when we know very well that under the roof of the high commissioner for the United Kingdom there was a woman who was a well known communist, who was found guilty and sen-

War Exchange Conservation

tenced, who had been a pink communist since 1932? Why have two weights and two measures? How is it that members of parliament are such sophomores that they ignore the fact that, while ambassadors and consuls may call themselves observers, they are only spies de luxe. They are accepted. The trouble with Russia was that they were looking through the keyhole; they showed bad manners, but others are spying just the same. Up to the time Canada declared war on Japan and the Japanese ambassador and his family returned to that country, there was no nest of intrigue and spying like the city of Ottawa, and everyone knows that.
Well, sir, here we are. It is a difficult matter, and the question is not to make a fine speech that will carry the house. The question is to see about the future. When we hear about human rights, fundamental freedoms, the improvement of health, et cetera, et cetera, how is it that we have so'much money to give to other countries, that we can look after the children of other countries but cannot look after those in our own country who are invalids, unless they are seventy years old or are blind? It is extraordinary. We have a lot to do, but before reforming other countries let us reform ourselves. Let us come down to brass tacks; let us be realists; let us do something for Canada before running ourselves for the benefit of other countries who pay no attention to us. In that connection the only thing to do is to think of our own country. There is so little freedom of speech that I am sure some newspapers will criticize the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Jaques) tomorrow because he said he was a nationalist. They will say he is such a short-sighted man, such a narrow-minded individual to describe himself in that way. Is this a bill of rights? Is this respect for liberty? I am ready to respect the liberty of everybody. I fight hard; I do not start a fight, but I can defend myself all right. But this is not an infringement upon the liberty of others. I respect the liberty of all, but I also want my liberty and freedom to be respected by all, which must be the feeling of everybody. If it is possible to awaken the House of Commons to its own responsibility there is no finer body of men in Canada. Then we will be able to go places and do something.
On motion of Mr. Hansell the debate was adjourned.
